lesson.text: Quick memory: what is a settlement? (A place where people live.) Wherever people live together, they need rules.
A rule tells people what to do or not to do. Families, classes, clubs and games all have rules. The rules a whole country must follow are called laws.
Why have rules? To keep people safe: walk, do not run, by the pool. To be fair: everyone takes turns. And to help things go smoothly: hands up to speak.
A fair rule is the same for everyone, is clear and has a good reason. It is made by listening to the people it is for. Voting can help a group choose.
Fair does not always mean the same. If Bram cannot reach the shelf, fair is giving him a step, not giving everyone a step. Fair means everyone gets what they need to have a good chance.

Children everywhere have rights. In 1989 the world's countries agreed the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child: every child has a right to be safe, to learn, to play, to be listened to, and to food and a home.
Rights come with responsibilities: if I have a right to be listened to, I listen to others too.
Try it in the world: with a friend, make three fair rules for a shared build in your world and put them on a sign. Does everyone agree they are fair?

exercises.hint: Think of the pool rule and taking turns.
choices: to keep people safe and be fair
so one person wins every time
exercises.explain: Rules keep people safe, make things fair and help a group run smoothly.

exercises.prompt: What are the rules a whole country must follow called?
exercises.hint: Judges and police officers look after them.
exercises.explain: The rules of a country are called laws.

exercises.prompt: A fair rule is the same for everyone.
exercises.hint: Would a rule for only some people feel fair?
exercises.explain: True: a fair rule applies to everyone in the group.

exercises.prompt: Every child in the world has a right to play.
exercises.hint: Remember the list the world's countries agreed in 1989.
exercises.explain: True: the Rights of the Child include the right to play and rest.

exercises.prompt: Which rule helps keep people safe?
exercises.hint: Which rule stops people getting hurt?
choices: walk, do not run, by the pool
only the tallest child can play
exercises.explain: Walking by the pool stops people slipping on the wet floor.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps for making a fair class rule in order.
exercises.hint: Ideas come first; the rule is written down last.
items: write the rule down for all
exercises.explain: Share ideas, listen to everyone, vote, then write the rule down so everyone knows it.

exercises.prompt: Which is a right from the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child?
exercises.hint: Rights are things every child needs, not things that would be nice.
choices: the right to stay up all night
the right to have a pony
the right to be the boss
exercises.explain: Every child has the right to learn, to be safe, to play and to be listened to.

exercises.prompt: A rule that only lets children with red hats play is fair.
exercises.hint: Is it the same for everyone? Does it have a good reason?
exercises.explain: False: it leaves others out for no good reason, so it is not fair.

exercises.prompt: Bram cannot reach the top shelf. What is fair?
exercises.hint: Fair means everyone gets what they need to have a good chance.
choices: give Bram a step so he can reach
give everyone a step, needed or not
exercises.explain: Giving Bram a step gives him what he needs, so he has the same chance as the others.

exercises.prompt: If I have the right to be listened to, what is my responsibility?
choices: to make others listen only to me
exercises.explain: If everyone has the right to be heard, each of us must listen to others too.

exercises.prompt: Voting lets everyone in a group have a say.
exercises.hint: What happens to each person's choice in a vote?
exercises.explain: True: in a vote, every person's choice is counted.

exercises.prompt: Mimi's friends argue about who goes first in a game. Which rule is fairest?
exercises.hint: Which rule gives everyone the same chance?
choices: take turns, and swap who starts
exercises.explain: Taking turns and swapping who starts gives everyone the same chance to go first.

exercises.prompt: In which year did the world's countries agree the Rights of the Child?
exercises.hint: It was in the late 1900s, not long ago in history.
exercises.explain: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child was agreed in 1989.

exercises.prompt: Match each child's right to an example of it.
exercises.hint: Think of what each right gives a child.
exercises.explain: Safe: grown-ups keep you from harm. Learn: school. Play: time for games and rest. Be listened to: your views are heard.

exercises.prompt: Sort the rules: fair or not fair?
items: Only Bram may use the slide.
exercises.hint: Is it the same for everyone, with a good reason?
exercises.explain: Taking turns and walking by the pool are the same for all, with good reasons. The other two are only for one person.

exercises.prompt: A class of 30 votes on a new rule. 18 vote yes. How many vote no?
exercises.hint: Everyone votes once: take the yes votes from 30.

exercises.prompt: Match each rule to its reason.
items: walk, don't run, by the pool
wear a helmet on a bike
exercises.hint: Rules keep people safe, keep things fair, or help things go smoothly.
exercises.explain: Walking by the pool stops slips, taking turns is fair, hands up helps things go smoothly, and a helmet keeps your head safe.

exercises.prompt: Fair means everyone gets what they need to have a good chance. Sort them: fair or not fair?
items: a step for Bram, who can't reach
glasses for a child who can't see well
help for a child learning English
the biggest slice for the loudest child
only the tallest child gets a turn
exercises.hint: Does it give someone what they need, or give someone more for no good reason?
exercises.explain: Fair: the step, the glasses and the extra English help each give someone what they need. Not fair: being loudest or tallest is no reason to get more.
